claims.text: Increasing Zr and Hf content in a high-entropy boride matrix improves resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The intervention is co-doping the boride with additional Zr and Hf to elevate their concentrations in the matrix.
The intended service condition is high-temperature exposure to molten aluminum typical of hot-dip aluminum plating.
The high-entropy boride can be processed by spark plasma sintering at approximately 2000 °C.
Spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed high-entropy boride powders at 2000 °C forms a single-phase hexagonal structure.
The proposed single-phase hexagonal high-entropy boride structure is enriched in Zr and Hf relative to the baseline.
Increasing Zr and Hf content increases the thermal-oxidative resistance of the high-entropy boride in gas-dynamic tests.
Increasing Zr and Hf content promotes formation of a more stable and protective oxide layer.
Increasing Zr and Hf content promotes compositional uniformity.
The protective oxide layer and compositional uniformity resist permeation by molten aluminum.
Resistance to molten-aluminum permeation reduces the corrosion rate.
The Zr/Hf-enriched material will have lower mass loss than a lower-Zr/Hf baseline after identical molten-aluminum exposure.
The Zr/Hf-enriched material will exhibit less corrosion depth and interfacial degradation than the baseline.
The corrosion-resistance benefit depends on processing that yields a homogeneous high-entropy boride phase.
Deviations in phase composition or significant impurities may negate the proposed corrosion-resistance benefit.
Improved thermal-oxidative resistance in gas-dynamic testing may not translate directly to resistance against molten-aluminum corrosion.
